title: Jonathan Knight's Meditative Series 'Exhale' Invites Us to Slow Down and Practice Noticing
description: “A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention,” economist and computer scientist Herbert Simon warned in 1971. In our era of digital ove
body:
“A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention,” economist and computer scientist Herbert Simon warned in 1971. In our era of digital overload, it feels increasingly urgent—ironically—to remember to slow down. Too often we’re distracted by one thing or the next, looking down at our screens or paying attention to our surroundings just briefly enough to snap a photo before moving on. Jonathan Knight is captivated instead by the quiet moments, the beauty in stillness, and the gentle, gradual changes around us that take time to fully appreciate.
Known for his ethereal, minimalist images, Knight conceived of Exhale as a way to explore the nuances of color and “the emotional experience of looking,” he says in a statement. On one hand, the photos are of water, but it may be more apt to describe them as portraits of atmosphere. Clear skies brimming with stars complement foggy mornings and a billowing release of rain from a heavy cloud. 

“The project grew out of my background in both photojournalism and landscape architecture, and from thinking about how we experience landscapes differently when we stop trying to document them and simply spend time with them,” Knight says. He adds:

There is also a technological tension at the heart of the work. We now live in a culture of instantaneous image-making, computational photography, AI-generated imagery, and endless visual consumption. Yet I’m deliberately using technology to do almost the opposite: to slow the photographic process down and make images that resist immediate consumption.

There is a sense of restraint in these images, where a lack of “flashiness” and few defining events lend a sense of the mundane. This is an invitation: through long exposure, both photographically and in the act of looking itself, Exhale invites us to practice noticing.
See more on Knight’s Instagram.

title: Gochman Collection of Indigenous Art to Open Katonah Space in November
description:
News
                The new home in New York, known as Branchline, will display selections from the family’s trove of over 800
body:
News
                The new home in New York, known as Branchline, will display selections from the family’s trove of over 800 contemporary Native artworks.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            From left to right: Rachel Martin, Becky Gochman, Audrey Lea Collins, Nicole van Brugge, Moonoka Begay, and Laura Phipps, of the Gochman Family Collection team (photo Denis Gutierrez-Ogrinc, courtesy Gochman Family Collection)
    
        
            Branchline, a permanent exhibition space for the Gochman Family Collection, will open on November 6 in Katonah, New York, functioning as a new home for the renowned trove of contemporary Native art.Building on the private collection's focus on Indigenous and anti-colonial art, Branchline will present rotating exhibitions of the over 800 works by contemporary Native artists in the Gochman Collection and provide residential and studio spaces for artists. Deriving its name from the network of rail lines that connect Katonah to surrounding areas like Manhattan and Upstate New York, Branchline also encompasses the ancestral and historical lineages informing the featured art."We imagine this as a flexible space to not only more broadly share the Collection, but to also create opportunities for varied audiences of artists, scholars, students, families, and our neighbors to spend time together," Laura Phipps, who became the collection's director in March, told Hyperallergic.Jeffrey Gibson's (Mississippi Band of Choctaw and Cherokee) "ACTION NOW ACTION IS ELOQUENCE" (2024) (photo Max Yawney, courtesy Gochman Family Collection)

title: Raven Chacon Sounds the History of the Land
description:
Interview
                The Pulitzer Prize-winning Diné artist talks about his recent performances at the Park Avenue Armory,
body:
Interview
                The Pulitzer Prize-winning Diné artist talks about his recent performances at the Park Avenue Armory, the freedom of improvisation, and the privilege of “deep listening.”
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Diné (Navajo) composer, performer, and visual artist Raven Chacon performs in the Veterans Room as part of Park Avenue Armory’s 2026 Artists Studio series on Wednesday, October 7. (all photos Da Ping Luo, courtesy Park Avenue Armory)
    
        
            On Wednesday and Thursday night, sound mixers, synthesizers, pedals, speakers, whistles, a turkey call, and a ceramic horn sat on a table at the center of the Veterans Room in Manhattan’s Park Avenue Armory. Serving as the stage for Raven Chacon’s hour-long improvisation sessions for the Armory’s Artists Studio series, the table also offered audiences the rare opportunity to see the prolific artist at play.During his performance on October 8, the Diné artist, composer, and Pulitzer Prize-winner used each object on the table to surprising and often discomfiting ends. He rigorously blew a whistle into a microphone, looping the sound and layering it atop a rising drone, which he intermittently cut to make room for the electronic transmission of the breath he recorded moments earlier. He mixed screeches over the whistles, eventually transforming the former into an oscillating, metallic sound redolent of the extraterrestrial signals in a sci-fi film. When the composition strayed too far into speculative abstraction, he’d snap it back with a clear, often frightening reminder of the world outside. Chacon ended the session by playing recordings of the wind through a hyperdirectional speaker that he moved in a circle around himself. He swept the sound of the wind over a new part of the room with each turn, transmitting with it the geography of alternative worlds much less violent than those sounded by the cars blaring up and down Park Avenue immediately outside, but whose continued existence depends upon our choosing to listen.I talked with Chacon over the phone between his performances at the Armory about the role of location in his work, his repurposing of tools associated with colonial violence, and his turn to science fiction for an upcoming show at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. Hyperallergic: For your Arts and Letters show, you were working with both local naturalist histories and the Lenape culture and history of New York. How do you bring site-specificity to a work like this that's entirely improvised?Raven Chacon: I wish I could say I was responding to the Armory [laughs]. When I’m playing in the city, I tend to bring in more field recordings of the outdoors, of wind and other sounds from other places. A lot of these were gathered where I'm from in New Mexico. While not site-specific to the Armory in this case, I find myself incorporating those more indoors, amongst the other things that encroach upon the interior of the space. It’s unavoidable that we might hear sirens and traffic outside, and those usually become part of the soundtrack of what I’m working with.H: Those sounds can have a different effect just based on the setting. We recently published a review of a group show you were in at the Hammer that likens your sound piece to a “California earthquake,” which is the type of resonance that you wouldn't get in New York.RC: That was certainly a consideration. Also, with that show, there were a lot of works about the actual ground. That installation was situated at the entry, but immediately, you have works by Edgar Calel, Ana Mendieta, these works that involve soil and dirt. I wanted to reference that with that piece. And as you move through, you have these different interactions with different materials and visual concepts happening throughout the show.Chacon working with synthesizers, mixers, and pedals during the session

title: Truman Lowe Listens to the Water
description:
Art Review
								In his first major retrospective, the Hoocąk artist transforms natural materials into fluid sculptures that carry the m
body:
Art Review
								In his first major retrospective, the Hoocąk artist transforms natural materials into fluid sculptures that carry the memory of place, ancestry, and cultural survival.
						
								
																
														
								
						
		
	  		    
        
            Truman Lowe, “Ottawa” (1992), pine, peeled wood saplings (all photos Chinyere Erondu/Hyperallergic)
    
		
				
						WASHINGTON, DC — Hoocąk (Ho-Chunk) artist Truman Lowe’s first major retrospective opens with “Ottawa” (1992), a billowing sculpture of pine and peeled willow saplings that brings together the tributary currents of the rivers that marked the aquatic realms of his childhood. The form undulates with an audacious disregard for the material’s inherent fixed state; each bend, movement, and ripple echoes Lowe’s unwavering ethos that wood is water.Throughout Water’s Edge: The Art of Truman Lowe at the National Museum of the American Indian, Lowe resonates with Toni Morrison’s sentiment that “all water has a perfect memory and is forever trying to get back to where it was.” The works are arranged around four themes of moving water: Landscape and Place, Woodland Structures, Memory, and Shared Knowledge. In Hoocąk culture, the number four holds reverence, history, and the recognition that repetition signifies permanence. This durability appears in multiple works by Lowe, such as “Mimi” (1979), a sculpture composed of four peeled willow branches, four groupings of blue jay feathers, and collections of red beads in sequences of four that cocoon the four strips of leather. Truman Lowe, “Wána (Cascade)" (2002), aluminium

title: Long Live Generation 6-7
description:
Weekly Newsletter

body:
Weekly Newsletter
                Lucy Ives reviews the Krasner-Pollock show at The Met, the L train burlesque arrives in Manhattan, photos from the student protests in France, and an interview with outgoing Yaddo President Elaina Richardson.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
    
        
            You try to get the latest news about the inspiring student protests in France but a snarky reporter on the New York Times podcast tells you that the country’s problem is providing “too generous” pension plans and parental leaves. These welfare benefits saddle the country with debt, he says, scolding the government for not making France more competitive in the marketplace. You turn off the podcast because you can’t listen to any more of this evil idiocy. You finally finish reading a much-hyped new novel and wonder why you made yourself go through such torture. You return to Marcel Proust’s In Search of Lost Time to cleanse your mind’s palette. “When one is in love one has no love left for anyone.”  You go to a gala dinner and remind yourself of the golden rule at these events: always go with the steak because you never know with chicken. You feel snazzy in your new tuxedo and remember that the last time you wore one was during the Arab Spring. You meet with Algerian-French artist Kader Attia in a Tunisian restaurant in Manhattan for an interview about a show he’s curating in India. His face full of wisdom and passion, he encourages you to wear your wounds on your sleeve.In the cold morning breeze, you see two doves perching on the wing of an eagle sculpture on a tall column. You think about how all good art has some connection to music, and how houses always look good when they’re painted green. Nina Simone sings “Tomorrow will be the 22nd century” in your ears. Meanwhile, generation 6-7 is remaking May 68.—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief 

	
		
		The Met’s Krasner and Pollock Show Is a Breathtaking Upending
		
	
	
		I was married to an artist once. It was not a good experience, although calling it “an experience” makes it sound like a unified, parsable thing, and it wasn’t that, either. We’re all adults here, is what I’m getting at — so no one should imagine that anyone has bulletproof insight into anyone else’s romantic relationship, much less their own. 
      
      Certainly, once a relationship is over, it becomes a moving target in permanence: the good, the bad, and the ugly all trading places, each a microcosm in which various genres of chaos and ecstasy hold sway. And whatever we may think of other people’s marriages, we must take care. What we believe we know is almost always something we meant to say about ourselves. The phone call is coming from inside the building. If you see something, well, see something. | Lucy Ives

title: 7 New York Exhibitions That Embody Indigenous Survivance
description:
Guide
                In shows coinciding with Indigenous Peoples' Day, artists including Jeremy Dennis, Shelley Niro, and Sarah
body:
Guide
                In shows coinciding with Indigenous Peoples' Day, artists including Jeremy Dennis, Shelley Niro, and Sarah Sense chart Native history and futurity.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Jeremy Dennis, “Manitou Hill” (2017) (photo courtesy the artist and the Long Island Museum)
    
        
            To commemorate Indigenous Peoples' Day here in New York, we have highlighted seven ongoing exhibitions of Native art and history in Manhattan, the Hessel Museum of Art at Bard College, and the Long Island Museum in Stony Brook. Across solo and group presentations, the featured artists, who represent a diverse tapestry of Indigenous populations across Turtle Island, embody survivance by tracing and rejecting narratives of dispossession and irrelevance, upending and satirizing stereotypes, preserving and reinventing traditional art forms, and bringing underrepresented histories out from the margins. Some of these sites are closed in observance of the occasion, and some of you have not been afforded the three-day weekend commanding this period of reflection, so rest assured that the following programs will be available from the last week of October through next spring.Cannupa Hanska Luger: American TraditionalGarth Greenan Gallery, 10 Greene Street, SoHo, ManhattanThrough Oct. 24Cannupa Hanska Luger, “American Traditional” (2026) (photo courtesy of the artist and Garth Greenan Gallery, New York)Inaugurating the gallery's new space, Cannupa Hanska Luger's (Mandan, Hidatsa, Arikara, and Lakota) American Traditional exchanges the artist's typically colorful verve for a series of uniform matte-black works born from ironstone clay, sumi ink, and direct flame. The titular work presents a striated sculpture of a skinned bison with a bifurcated skull sitting on a standard colonial-fashion dining table. Encoded in tautly wrapped yarn, this distortion manifests throughout Luger's wall hangings and pedestals of other animal skulls and carcasses, which are embellished with railroad spikes, Pulaski axes, and vintage “American Traditional” furniture associated with the westward settler expansion. Per the artist, the work emphasizes the “bizarre and horrific history of colonialism,” and the motifs of mutilation and mutation speak to the manipulation of collective memory in the retelling and neglect of certain perspectives. Shelley Niro: In Her LifetimeHales Gallery, 547 West 20th Street, Chelsea, ManhattanThrough Oct. 31Shelley Niro, “Queen Bees” (1991) (© Shelley Niro; photo JSP Art Photography, courtesy Hales | London and New York)Turtle Clan of the Kanyen’kehá:ka (Mohawk) Nation artist and filmmaker Shelley Niro celebrates her second solo show with Hales New York in a tight selection of mixed-media photographic works spanning decades of her career. In Her Lifetime, which takes its name from Niro's 1992 black-and-white picture sequence of her sister with overlaid text, emphasizes the artist's use of humor and accessible references in her personal reflections on identity, nationhood, collective memory, and stereotypes through an Indigenous perspective. For this exhibition, Niro also reinterprets a variety of her iconic photos from the early 1990s, embellishing them with hand-painted elements and decorative patterns that, in the context of Indigenous womanhood, add a certain cheeky assertiveness to her family portrayals.

title: Alex Margo Arden Gets Up Close and Personal With Amy Winehouse’s Items for an Exhibition in London
description: This summer marked 15 years since the death of British singer-songwriter Amy Winehouse, but her spirit lives on. Now, her life and influence are the
body:
This summer marked 15 years since the death of British singer-songwriter Amy Winehouse, but her spirit lives on. Now, her life and influence are the subject of “Nothing Personal,” a just-opened exhibition by artist Alex Margo Arden spread across three rooms of the Nicoletta Fiorucci Foundation in London.

	For the exhibition, Arden has created hundreds of simulacra of Winehouse’s personal items, recreating a pair of ballet slippers signed by fans left outside the singer’s home after her death and a birthday card from the music producer Mark Ronson and Adele that Winehouse never received. To round out this display, Arden purchased exact copies of books found in Winehouse’s library, the makeup and perfume she used, and boardgames and decorative items like mirrors that dotted her house. The display can at times feel like you’re surreptitiously browsing the most intimate parts of someone’s home. Since 2021, Arden has been forensically dissecting pixelated images of Winehouse she’s found online, in catalogues, newspapers and magazines, to determine which items she would need to track down. 
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	“This show is a really personal insight into Amy,” Arden told ARTnews, describing what’s on view as “parallel objects.” She feels that the hundred books on display create an intimate atmosphere and add historical value, more so than if she actually had presented just one or two authentic items from Winehouse’s estate.


			
			
			
	
			
					Alex Margo Arden, Library, 2026.
									Courtesy the artist
	



	The sensitivity to detail across the project is striking. At one point during this five-year scavenger hunt, Arden wound up with 20 versions of the same book; she wanted to compare each copy’s spine and cover to make sure she had the correct one. The bulk of this labor is showcased in Library (2026), containing dozens of tomes from Vladimir Nabokov’s Speak Memory next to the cookbook The New Classic 1000 Recipes, which is not far from a book on marriage. There are also biographies of David Beckham, Bob Dylan, Carole King, Marilyn Monroe, and Audrey Hepburn.

	“What I’m proposing in the artwork is that as a collection, this gives us really good insight” into Winehouse’s life, Arden said, warning against zeroing in on any one book. She pointed to a Weight Watchers book, which some might relate to Winehouse’s history of eating disorders, which were put under a microscope by the British tabloids. “In isolation, these objects can be used to really push specific narratives about her,” she explained.
	

	In the next room, Arden presents Same Otherwise (2026), a recreation of the fireplace in Winehouse’s home at 2 Jeffrey’s Place, where she wrote her Grammy Award–winning album Back to Black. Just as Winehouse once had it, Arden has positioned framed issues of British Vogue, comic book pages from Betty and Veronica, and a mirror with a picture of Marilyn Monroe over the mantel. But the artist has left gaps where the musician had personal photos of friends and family framed. “The gaps speak to the feeling of things being present and missing always,” she said.


			
			
			
	
			
					Alex Margo Arden, Perfume said to have belonged to Amy Winehouse [I-IV], 2024–26.
									Courtesy of Alex Margo Arden
	



	As we spoke, I became captivated by a scent in the gallery. At first I thought it was Arden’s perfume, but the fragrance was, in fact, an artwork, Perfume said to have belonged to Amy Winehouse [I-IV] (2024–26). The Chanel No.5 I was smelling had been emitted from a custom dispenser by Arden. Throughout the exhibition’s run, the Chanel No.5 will be exchanged for other perfumes that Winehouse is said to have worn. Arden wouldn’t disclose which ones would feature, but various accounts by fashion publications previously reported that Winehouse also wore Alien by Thierry Mugler, Vera Wang Princess, and Givenchy’s Hot Couture. The work was a touching reminder of Winehouse’s tangible presence, wafting through the galleries.
	

	The exhibition also includes more intimate works that at times get overshadowed. Jigsaw (2026), for example, is a stack of those titular puzzles of scenes of the Beatles, The Simpsons, and Casablanca. The patience required to piece them together paints Winehouse as an introspective woman as opposed to her party girl that the tabloids portrayed her as. Sent Otherwise (2026) is the recreation of the aforementioned birthday card that was only discovered years later, a poignant reminder that even a decade and a half after Winehouse’s death, her life is still being excavated. Taken together, they act as clever tidbits into Winehouse’s short-lived life.

	To her tribute to Winehouse, Arden also adds a piece of herself, via Display Identification Cubes (2026), an artwork made up of a thousand acrylic ice cubes that resemble the placards that are typically used in museum vitrines to match an object to its corresponding label. This numbering methodology recurs across Arden’s oeuvre. In All Clear (2022), these numbers appear as print-outs affixed next to items such as a broom, a ladder, and a woven basket, perhaps evoking the objects found at a crime scene, the mundane taking on a more sinister connotation. 

	But in “Nothing Personal,” on view through January 23, the plastic numbers serve as pieces that Arden hasn’t discovered about Winehouse yet—and maybe never will. “They draw attention to spaces where things are absent, but they also mark spaces where things have once been,” she said.
